title: How to Connect With Anyone
author: Josue Valles
summary: Josue Valles uses a single story to make a pointed argument about building relationships with hard-to-reach people. A friend who moved from Tokyo to Los Angeles with three children and little money joined the most expensive public golf course he could afford and showed up every Saturday at sunrise. Because early solo golfers are paired with strangers, he met a new group of executives every week and built his core network within six months, despite being a poor golfer. Valles draws the lesson that the sport was incidental; what mattered was long, unhurried shared time in a setting the target community already enjoys. He contrasts this with saturated channels designed explicitly for networking, such as conferences, LinkedIn messages, and cold emails, and urges readers to find the equivalent spaces for their own audiences.
points: Channels built explicitly for networking, like conferences, LinkedIn messages, and cold emails, are saturated and yield little with busy, senior people.
Golf worked because sunrise tee times pair solo players with strangers, creating a weekly rotation of executives and four hours of conversation.
The transferable principle is to identify what your target community already enjoys and join them there, whether a cyclists' coffee shop or a padel court.
Trust grows faster through hours of shared downtime than through short, forced networking meetings.
quotes: In 2012, a friend of mine moved from Tokyo to LA with 3 kids and just $20,000 in his bank account. He didn’t know anyone, so he joined the most expensive public golf course he could afford and showed up every Saturday morning.
Within 6 months, he built his core LA network entirely on that fairway. Investors, advisors, and future partners who would never reply to a cold email happily chatted with him on the back nine.

Successful executives (the exact people he needed to meet) tee off at sunrise on Saturdays so they can finish by 11 AM to spend time with their families. Since early morning golfers often arrive solo, the course starter pairs them with 3 strangers.
A 4-hour round creates the time and space for genuine conversations about life, business, and family. It wasn’t the sport itself that made the difference, but the environment.

It’s that if you’re trying to build relationships with “unreachable” people, you shouldn’t rely on channels explicitly designed for networking (conferences, LinkedIn messages, cold emails, etc.). Those are saturated.
You build far more genuine trust over a few hours of shared downtime than you ever will in a forced fifteen-minute coffee chat.
